content.title: EBOLA BUNDIBUGYO VIRUS DISEASE OUTBREAK Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 23, Data as of 19 October 2026
content.abstract: EBOLA BUNDIBUGYO VIRUS DISEASE OUTBREAK Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 23, Data as of 19 October 2026 orlunwop@who.int Wed, 21/10/2026 - 14:33 The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak is becoming increasingly challenging, marked by an expanding cluster of cases linked to the imported index case in Kenya, further geographic expansion into a new province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and the confirmation of a case in Nigeria. These developments highlight the widening international dimension and the growing complexity of the outbreak, particularly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where escalating insecurity, population displacement and restricted humanitarian access threaten to further undermine surveillance and response operations. Democratic Republic of the Congo As of 19 October 2026, the BVD outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has affected 66 health zones across eight provinces, following the recent expansion into Wapinda Health Zone in Nord-Ubangi Province. Since External Situation Report #22, an additional 572 confirmed cases and 265 confirmed deaths have been reported, bringing the cumulative total to 9637 confirmed cases, including 4646 confirmed deaths [crude case fatality ratio (CFR) 48.2%]. Transmission remains highly heterogeneous across affected areas. Ituri continues to account for the largest proportion of cumulative confirmed cases (72.7%), although its relative contribution is declining, while substantial transmission persists in Nord-Kivu and Haut-Uélé. content.title: Global mpox outbreak dynamics during and after the 2024-2026 public health emergency.
content.abstract: The second WHO Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) for mpox was declared on 14 August 2024 after clade Ib monkeypox virus emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and spread rapidly across Africa and internationally. The PHEIC ended on 5 September 2025, and the Africa CDC Public Health Emergency of Continental Security was lifted on 22 January 2026. This study characterised global and Africa-specific mpox epidemiology across the full second PHEIC cycle and immediate post-emergency period, from January 2024 to February 2026. A retrospective surveillance analysis was conducted using the WHO Global Mpox Trends dashboard exported data, supplemented by WHO situation reports S32-S64 and international and national surveillance reports. Analyses included negative binomial segmented regression, travel-linked pathway analysis, exploratory analysis of documented secondary transmission after travel-linked detection, and descriptive statistics. Models used reported case counts with log population offsets; reported case-rate ratios therefore reflect reported case rates rather than true infection incidence. Between January 2024 and February 2026, 82,738 confirmed cases and 306 deaths were reported to WHO globally (case fatality ratio 0.37%). The PHEIC period accounted for 74.0% of cases, peaking at 7,405 cases in May 2025. In total, 163 clade-specific importation or travel-linked detection events were documented across 41 countries within the primary analytic cutoff; documented secondary transmission occurred in 25 (15.3%) events across 16 countries. Within DRC, 200 health zones recorded 144,035 total reported cases and 2,047 deaths (case fatality ratio 1.42%); these aggregate suspected/clinically compatible and confirmed cases. The top 20 health zones accounted for 45.4% of national burden. Reported transmission declined after the May 2025 peak but persisted beyond PHEIC termination. Emergency termination marked an administrative transition, not the end of mpox transmission. The post-emergency period requires sustained surveillance, maintained diagnostic capacity, targeted response in persistent transmission settings, and equitable access to vaccines and countermeasures.

content.title: Fatal Occupational Leptospirosis in a Beef Cattle Farmer: Case Report and Epidemiological Investigation.
content.abstract: Leptospirosis is a re-emerging zoonosis responsible for approximately 1 million human infections and 59,000 deaths annually worldwide. In Europe, notification rates have increased by 5% per year since 2010, a trend compounded by climate change. The study was performed to document a fatal occupational case acquired through an under-recognised environmental exposure pathway, and to establish what regional surveillance data can and cannot support regarding its burden and exposure profile. We report a fatal case of occupational leptospirosis in a 56-year-old male beef cattle farmer in Lombardy (Po Valley, Italy) and describe the subsequent epidemiological investigation. Regional surveillance data, veterinary notifications, ECDC data, and an analysis of occupational and climate-related exposure pathways were reviewed. The index case was caused by a strain of serogroup Javanica (microscopic agglutination test titre 1:3,200 against serovar Poi), absent from standard regional animal serological screening panels, probably acquired through contaminated irrigation water. Among 16 confirmed leptospirosis cases in Lombardy over 22 months, 3 (18.8%) died and 1 (6.3%) had permanent disability (severe-outcome rate 25.0%, likely an underestimate given surveillance failures). Twelve of 16 cases (75.0%) had an agricultural-environmental exposure nexus. Leptospirosis risk in irrigated agriculture extends beyond livestock contact to environmental contamination of surface water by wildlife reservoirs. Climate change is expected to expand the disease's European distribution and extend the transmission season. A One Health approach integrating occupational medicine, veterinary surveillance, engineering controls, and climate-adaptive prevention is needed.

content.title: Resurgence of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo: Lessons Learned and Future Directions.
content.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) remains the global epicenter of Ebola virus disease (EVD), having experienced more than 15 outbreaks since the disease was first identified in 1976. The 2025 resurgence in Kasai Province, caused by Orthoebolavirus zairense, resulted in over 60 confirmed cases and a case fatality rate exceeding 65%, highlighting persistent vulnerabilities in outbreak preparedness and response despite previous control successes. This article examines the drivers, response strategies, and public health implications of the 2025 Ebola outbreak. METHODS: This perspective synthesizes evidence from publicly available reports, epidemiological updates, genomic surveillance findings, and guidance from national and international public health agencies to examine the epidemiological characteristics, health system challenges, response interventions, and lessons learned from the 2025 Ebola outbreak in the DRC. RESULTS: Genomic evidence suggested viral persistence in human reservoirs as a likely source of the outbreak. Delayed diagnosis due to limited laboratory capacity, reagent shortages, and slow sample transportation impeded timely case confirmation. Sociocultural factors, including unsafe burial practices, vaccine hesitancy, and community mistrust, further complicated containment efforts. The outbreak overwhelmed fragile health systems, with inadequate isolation facilities and personal protective equipment contributing to healthcare worker infections, which accounted for 10% of reported cases. Coordinated national and international interventions, including emergency response activation, ring vaccination with the rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP (Ervebo) vaccine, enhanced surveillance, contact tracing, infection prevention and control measures, and technical support from global partners, were instrumental in interrupting transmission. CONCLUSION: The 2025 Ebola outbreak demonstrates the continued threat of recurrent EVD in the DRC and underscores the need for resilient surveillance systems, decentralized laboratory capacity, sustained infection prevention and control measures, healthcare worker protection, meaningful community engagement, and strengthened regional collaboration. Integrating genomic surveillance and advancing vaccine research will be critical for improving epidemic preparedness and strengthening health security across Central Africa.

content.title: Characterization of an Unusual Severe Yellow Fever Outbreak in the Colombian Andean Region.
content.abstract: BACKGROUND: Yellow fever (YF) reemerged in Colombia's Andean region during 2024-2025, outside the country's historically recognized endemic areas. We characterized critically ill adults admitted during this outbreak and described clinical features, organ dysfunction, supportive care, and in-hospital outcomes. METHODS: We conducted a prospective observational cohort study of consecutive adults with reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR)-confirmed YF admitted to the national referral intensive care unit in Ibagué, Tolima, Colombia, from March through September 2025. Clinical, laboratory, complication, intervention, and outcome data were prospectively captured using a standardized case report form. RESULTS: Sixty-one patients were analyzed; 22 died (36.1%). Non-survivors had lower platelet counts and fibrinogen and higher INR, aminotransferases, lactate dehydrogenase, and creatinine at ICU admission. Shock, acute kidney injury, acute respiratory distress syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and severe bleeding were more frequent among non-survivors. Prior YF vaccination was self-reported by 10 patients (16.4%). CONCLUSIONS: Severe YF in this Andean outbreak was characterized by hepatic-coagulation abnormalities and multisystem organ dysfunction. The occurrence of critical illness outside historically recognized endemic areas supports surveillance and vaccination strategies that can adapt to changing epidemiological risk.

content.title: Mammary Gland Tropism and Milk-Mediated Transmission of H5N1 in Dairy Cattle: Implications for One Health Surveillance.
content.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 virus (H5N1 HPAIV) has long circulated in wild waterfowl and poultry and continues to cross species barriers, posing sustained threats to livestock productivity and public health. The 2024 outbreak of H5N1 HPAIV in dairy cattle across multiple U.S. states represents the first recognized large-scale transmission event of this virus in ruminants, reshaping our understanding of its host range and transmission ecology. This review summarizes recent advances in the epidemiology, virological characteristics, transmission, pathogenesis, surveillance, and control of dairy cattle-associated H5N1. The initial multistate outbreak was dominated by clade 2.3.4.4b genotype B3.13, whereas subsequent independent introductions of genotype D1.1 demonstrated that repeated avian-to-cattle spillover also contributes to the evolving outbreak ecology. A defining feature is efficient replication in bovine mammary epithelial cells, resulting in high viral titers in milk, supporting milk-associated exposure and milking-related contamination as plausible components of transmission, although the relative contribution of different routes remains unresolved. Infected cattle typically show reduced feed intake, a marked decline in milk production, abnormal milk, and mild systemic signs, whereas severe respiratory disease and mortality are uncommon. Mutations such as PB2-M631L, PA-K497R, and changes in NP and NS1 may promote replication and immune evasion in bovine cells, while genotype-specific PB2 adaptations highlight the potential for further mammalian adaptation. Human infections reported to date have been predominantly mild and associated with occupational exposure, with no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission. Experimental vaccine studies have begun to demonstrate immunogenicity in cattle, although protection against mammary infection, viral shedding, and transmission remains to be established. Future priorities include clarifying mammary tropism and transmission dynamics, while strengthening diagnostics, farm biosecurity, vaccination, evaluating cattle vaccination strategies, and integrated One Health surveillance.

content.title: Avian cholera causes mass mortality at penguin mega-colonies amid H5N1 HPAI outbreaks in Antarctica.
content.abstract: The characterization of pathogens affecting Antarctic wildlife has been historically limited and sporadic. With the introduction of H5N1 high pathogenicity avian influenza virus (HPAIV) in Antarctica in the austral summer 2023/2024, concerns about the health of Antarctic seabirds and mammals prompted immediate surveillance efforts. In March 2024, we visited the Danger Islands archipelago, that hosts two mega-colonies of Adélie penguins, and observed an unusual mortality estimated in thousands of Adélie penguins and other species. Swabs and tissues were collected for molecular detection of infectious agents from 49 carcasses, and additional tissues for histology from a selection of 9 carcasses. We detected Pasteurella multocida DNA in 46 of 49 individuals, and diagnosed avian cholera as the cause of death of most of these animals. By shotgun sequencing, we retrieved the first genomic sequences of the P. multocida strain from this region, and the phylogenetic analysis showed a close relation with strains from other locations retrieved during the same expedition and with strains previously reported in the Southern Ocean area. This study confirms avian cholera as a relevant cause of mortality in the Antarctic, and overall highlights the importance of considering this disease in the differential diagnoses during mortality events in Antarctica.

content.title: Imported chikungunya in French travelers returning from outbreak-affected regions.
content.abstract: BACKGROUND: Outbreaks of chikungunya disease are unpredictable, typically episodic, and explosive. In 2025, several such outbreaks were observed and a marked increase in imported cases of chikungunya to mainland France was reported. This study aimed to describe the rate of chikungunya in French travelers returning from La Réunion, Mayotte, Mauritius, Madagascar, Sri Lanka, and Cuba, all of which showed major chikungunya resurgences in 2025, and to assess the potential burden that CHIKV outbreaks-whether officially notified or not-can cause to travelers. METHODS: Publicly available data from Santé Publique France were used to extract the number of chikungunya cases, and International Air Transport Association data were used for information on the number of flight tickets to estimate traveler numbers. These data were used to derive monthly rates of imported cases of chikungunya to mainland France from January to December 2025. RESULTS: Trends in rates of chikungunya among travelers returning to mainland France from La Réunion and Mayotte closely mirrored the sharp and compact epidemic curves observed locally. Peak imported rates exceeded 1,800 cases/100,000 travelers (La Réunion [April]) and 400 cases/100,000 travelers (Mayotte [May]) and remained above 100 cases/100,000 travelers for March, April, May, and June (La Réunion) and April, May, and June (Mayotte). For Mauritius, Madagascar, Sri Lanka, and Cuba, estimated peak rates were 248, 338, 90, and 2,480 cases/100,000 travelers, respectively, although it was noted that some outbreaks were not officially notified or were reported late. CONCLUSIONS: Returning travelers to mainland France from regions facing a chikungunya outbreak in 2025 showed a substantial burden of infection and gave rise to local spread of disease, highlighting the importance of robust surveillance systems and timely outbreak notification.

content.title: No receptor-binding domain adaptation detected in within-host H5N1 surveillance of 4,559 US dairy outbreak sequences.
content.abstract: BACKGROUND: The 2024-2026 US H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b dairy cattle outbreak has been characterised primarily through consensus-level phylogenetics. Whether mammalian-adaptation variants are emerging at sub-consensus frequencies within infected hosts, particularly at the haemagglutinin receptor-binding domain (RBD), remains unknown because no systematic within-host variant analysis of the public sequencing corpus has been performed. METHODS: We conducted a pre-registered, corpus-wide intrahost single-nucleotide variant (iSNV) analysis of all publicly available H5N1 cattle, feline-spillover, and retail-milk sequences on the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (4559 samples across 7 BioProjects). A dual-caller concordance pipeline (iVar + LoFreq) with empirically determined allele frequency (AF) threshold (3%, set via four-criterion validation including synthetic spike-in controls) was applied to an 11-site Tier 1 mammalian-adaptation panel spanning the polymerase complex, haemagglutinin RBD, and accessory proteins. Within-host nucleotide diversity was compared across host categories. RESULTS: The HA RBD sites Q226L and G228S (H3 numbering) showed zero detections across >4300 adequately sequenced samples at all AF thresholds tested (1-5%), despite the pipeline detecting other non-synonymous variants at these exact codon positions (upper 95% CI for prevalence: 0.08%). Seven of eleven adaptation sites carried statistically significant iSNV signals after Bonferroni correction (corrected α = 0.00417), though all at low prevalence (≤2.95%). Genotype stratification showed that most polymerase-site detections reflected genotype structure rather than within-host emergence: the apparent PB2 631 L→M "reversion" was largely the ancestral avian state of the D1.1 genotype (20 of 23 detections), which never acquired the 631L mammalian adaptation, with only two genuine sub-consensus events in the B3.13 background, while consensus-level PB2 701N was a fixed feature of the D1.1 genotype (10 of 14 detections) rather than independent sub-consensus emergence. Cattle exhibited significantly higher within-host nucleotide diversity than feline-spillover samples (π = 1.59 × 10-4 vs 6.11 × 10-5; Kruskal-Wallis p = 6.6 × 10-15), a finding that persisted after depth-matching (p = 4.6 × 10-5); this may reflect prolonged mammary-gland infection, though sampling differences and host biology cannot be excluded. CONCLUSIONS: We did not detect HA receptor-switching adaptation (the acquisition of human-type α2,6 receptor binding via Q226L/G228S) at any tested allele frequency in the US dairy H5N1 outbreak. Sub-consensus mammalian-adaptation signals exist at polymerase-complex sites but at low prevalence, are genotype-structured rather than independently recurrent, and require functional characterisation before informing risk assessment.

content.title: First detection and characterization of a non-haemadsorbing African swine fever virus (genotype II) isolated from a wild boar in Russia.
content.abstract: In 2023, a non-haemadsorbing African swine fever virus (ASFV) of genotype II (isolate ASFV/Kirov/WB2023/1448) was recovered from a wild boar in the Kirov Region of Russia-the first such case during the current epidemic (2007-present). Whole-genome analysis of the non-haemadsorbing ASFV revealed a large deletion (~1,300 base pairs) in the EP153R and EP402R genes, and a smaller deletion (~50 base pairs) in the MGF 110-1 L gene. Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that ASFV/Kirov/WB2023/1448 belongs to the genetic lineage «II/EU1/RU7», which is typical for the European part of Russia. Following intramuscular inoculation of eight domestic pigs with isolate ASFV/Kirov/WB2023/1448 at a dose of 103 TCID50 moderate virulence was observed, with the development of acute and subacute forms of ASF. Furthermore, the non-haemadsorbing virus was shown to be contagious, as two pigs maintained in direct contact with the inoculated animals developed ASF. The mortality rate among pigs infected via the intramuscular and contact routes was 60%. Two out of ten infected pigs recovered from ASF; persistence of the non-haemadsorbing virus was not detected, as complete elimination of the virus from the host organism was observed within 28 days post-infection. Upon challenge of the recovered pigs with the highly virulent haemadsorbing isolate ASFV/Kirov/WB2023/1447-which had been recovered from the same wild boar population as ASFV/Kirov/WB2023/1448-the animals exhibited no clinical signs of disease, viraemia, virus shedding, or virus dissemination in organs and tissues. To investigate the possible circulation of the non-haemadsorbing virus in wildlife, 122 field samples collected from hunted and found-dead wild boars within a single population in Kirov Region and adjacent regions of the Russian Federation during the period 2021-2023 were examined. Two hunted animals sampled in 2023 in the Republic of Mari El (bordering Kirov Region) were found to be seropositive with no detectable ASFV. The present study may indicate the emergence of natural mechanisms of virulence attenuation of ASFV genotype II in the European wild boar population over a relatively short period of pathogen circulation (15-16 years).

content.title: Fetal arrhythmia and heart disease during COVID-19 pandemic in patients who underwent echocardiography.
content.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the characteristics and the occurrence of fetal heart diseases and arrhythmias in pregnancies that underwent fetal echocardiography examination during COVID-19 pandemic. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data extracted from the Fetal Ultrasound and Fetal Medicine Departments of Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein, a tertiary hospital in São Paulo, Brazil, from January to December 2021. The sample was analyzed using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, and Student's t-test or the Mann-Whitney test. Logistic regression was performed to assess the risk of fetal arrhythmia and/or heart disease. RESULTS: A total of 148 fetuses were included in the analysis. The prevalence of fetal heart disease/arrhythmia was higher among patients with maternal comorbidities (73.3% vs. 39.1%), fetal defects (14.3% vs. 0.8%), and functional abnormalities (26.7% vs. 4.5%). Maternal COVID-19 showed no significant association with fetal cardiac outcomes. Maternal comorbidity, fetal malformation, and the presence of functional abnormalities were identified as independent risk factors. CONCLUSION: Maternal comorbidities were associated with fetal arrhythmia and/or heart disease, but no causal relationship was found between COVID-19 and adverse fetal cardiac outcome.

content.title: Genetic Diversity of Clade 2.3.4.4b H5Nx high pathogenicity Avian Influenza Viruses detected in Korea during the 2025-2026 winter season and pathogenicity of H5N1 and H5N9 viruses.
content.abstract: Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1, H5N6, and H5N9 high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs) were detected in poultry and wild birds during the 2025-2026 winter season in Korea. During this period, 62 H5Nx HPAI outbreaks occurred in poultry, and 63 cases were reported in wild birds. Genome constellation analysis revealed substantial genotype diversity. Most H5N1 and H5N9 genotypes were reassortants containing gene segments derived from East Asian clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 HPAIVs since 2022 and low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses from wild birds. Notably, the European H5N1 genotype EA-2024-DI.2.1, which spread rapidly across Europe in 2025, and its reassortants were identified in Korea. The novel poultry genotypes were also detected in wild birds, supporting wild bird to poultry spillover, whereas one genotype detected in previous season was identified in small-scale poultry farms. H5N1 (C588) of major 25G2 genotype in poultry and H5N9 (C722) of N9-G2 genotype showed high infectivity in chickens with 103.3 and 103.2 EID50 of median lethal dose (LD50) values, respectively. The predominance of the 25G2 genotype in poultry may have been influenced by efficient infection and virus introduction into high-density poultry production areas, potentially facilitating horizontal transmission under field conditions. In young ducks, H5N1 caused rapid mortality, whereas H5N9 induced limited clinical signs without mortality. Both viruses were transmitted to all contact ducks, increasing the risk of transmission to poultry. Despite intensified surveillance and early detection efforts to limit virus spread, H5Nx HPAIV outbreaks occurred during the 2025-2026 winter season. These findings highlight the need for continued surveillance, together with rapid genomic and pathogenic characterization of newly introduced viruses.

content.title: Imported mixed malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium ovalecurtisi: An Italian case report.
content.abstract: Malaria remains a major global health threat, particularly in endemic regions of sub-Saharan Africa. In 2024 alone, an estimated 282 million cases were reported worldwide, with approximately 610,000 associated deaths. Beyond the high disease burden, mixed-species Plasmodium infections represent an additional clinical challenge, as they are frequently underdiagnosed and may significantly complicate both diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic management even in non-endemic countries. We report the case of a 67-year-old man from Guinea who presented to the Emergency Department with high-grade fever and asthenia shortly after returning to Italy; initial microbiological investigations were negative, despite markedly elevated inflammatory markers were diagnosed. The patient reported a previous untreated malaria episode approximately six months earlier, raising suspicion of a novel Plasmodium infection. A comprehensive malaria diagnostic workflow was promptly initiated, integrating rapid immunoenzymatic testing (IE), microscopy, and molecular assays. The IE test suggested Plasmodium falciparum or a mixed infection as result, while loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP-PCR) confirmed the presence of Plasmodium spp DNA. Microscopic examination of stained blood smears revealed typical P. falciparum ring forms and suspected P. ovale trophozoites; so, species-specific real-time PCR confirmed a mixed infection with P. falciparum and P. ovale, supporting prompt antimalarial treatment. Final molecular confirmation was achieved by Sanger sequencing, which identified the Plasmodium ovalecurtisi as co-aetiological agent of disease. The rapid and integrated diagnostic approach enabled timely initiation of appropriate antimalarial therapy with artemether-lumefantrine and primaquine, leading to complete clinical recovery and gene sequencing allowed a correct species confirmation and epidemiological characterization. This case highlights the importance of combining microscopic analysis with advanced molecular diagnosis for an accurate identification of mixed Plasmodium infections even in country and contributes novel epidemiological data through molecular characterization of P. ovalecurtisi in an imported case.

content.title: Characterization of norovirus GI.3 and GII.12 variants detected in wastewater: proof-of-concept for integrating phenotypic insights in wastewater-based epidemiology.
content.abstract: UNLABELLED: Norovirus is the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis, responsible for 685 million cases and 200,000 deaths annually. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) enables not only global surveillance of dominant strains but also the detection of cryptic and emerging viral variants. An important question, however, is how to link genomic diversity to clinical impact and phenotypic traits of the strains detected in wastewater. In the Global Urban Wastewater Project, phylogenetically distinct norovirus GI.3 and GII.12 lineages were detected in wastewater from Cameroon. In this study, we characterized their host- and tissue-binding specificity and antigenic makeup in comparison with other GI.3 and GII.12 lineages using a luciferase immunoprecipitation system-based assay, alongside sequence analysis of the VP1 P2 subdomain. We observed intra-genotype variation among GI.3 variants. GI.3 Cameroon/2017 shared phenotypes with its closest reference strain (GI.3 Mexico/2016), and their histo-blood group antigen (HBGA)-binding profiles suggested a narrower susceptible population compared to other GI.3 lineages. Conversely, GII.12 strains showed no significant differences in HBGA binding, antigenic profiles, and tissue attachment. Together, these results reveal distinct patterns of phenotypic diversity between the two genotypes. While GI.3 variants exhibited lineage-specific traits, the GII.12 strains appeared phenotypically conserved across lineages. These findings highlight the feasibility and importance of integrating phenotypic analysis with WBE to assess potential public health risks posed by novel viral variants. IMPORTANCE: While detection of norovirus through case-based surveillance is limited to variants causing symptomatic infection, wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) allows for detection of cryptic and emerging variants. However, validation, such as phenotypic characterization, is needed to assess the clinical importance of a variant detected in WBE. In this study, we investigated the phenotypic traits of genetically distinct GI.3 and GII.12 lineages detected in wastewater from Cameroon. We utilized NanoLuc luciferase immunoprecipitation system (N-LIPS)-based assays to assess binding specificity and antigenicity. Compared to traditional methods involving virus isolation and virus-like particle production, N-LIPS-based assays are considerably less laborious and faster. This allows for rapid characterization of novel variants, making the timely assessment of phenotypic changes of such variants for outbreak or pandemic preparedness feasible. Finally, by integrating insights from phenotypic assays, we showed the possibility of expanding the public health value of wastewater surveillance in assessing the risk of novel viral variants.

content.title: Large-scale fever screening based on infrared thermography for outpatients at tertiary medical center during COVID-19 pandemic: implementation and practical experience.
content.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the clinical utility of a multi-step fever screening program using infrared thermography (IRT) for visitors to outpatient clinics at a tertiary care hospital during the COVID-19 pandemic. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, retrospective study at The University of Tokyo Hospital between January and December 2022, when the Omicron variant was predominant. Outpatient visitors underwent a three-step screening at the main entrance, including IRT, axillary temperature measurement, and physician's evaluation. Outcomes included the number of COVID-19 cases detected, the positive predictive value (PPV) of IRT, and its association with ambient air temperature. RESULTS: Of 570,076 asymptomatic visitors screened by IRT, 3900 (0.7%) had a body temperature ≥ 37.0 °C; among them, 483 (12.4%) had axillary temperatures ≥ 37.0 °C. In total, 115 visitors (0.02%) were evaluated by physicians, and 55 underwent PCR testing, of whom 2 tested positive. The PPV of IRT was 12.4% and showed a strong correlation with ambient temperature (r = 0.93). CONCLUSIONS: The overall yield of IRT-based fever screening at a tertiary hospital was minimal, with only 1 COVID-19 case detected per approximately 285,000 (2/570,076). Our findings highlight the limited clinical utility of fever-based screening and emphasize the importance of carefully considering disease characteristics, environmental factors, and resource allocation in future pandemic preparedness.

content.title: Cluster investigation report: a probable urine-associated transmission event of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome-a case report.
content.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging tick-borne viral disease with a high case fatality rate. Human-to-human transmission has been increasingly documented, primarily through direct contact with blood or bloody secretions. On June 21, 2025, a case of SFTS was reported in Zhumadian City, Henan Province. On July 3, a second case-epidemiologically linked to the first-was reported to the local Centers for Disease Control (CDC) through the notifiable disease reporting system, following laboratory confirmation on July 1. CASE PRESENTATION: A 77-year-old female farmer with underlying comorbidities was hospitalized with fever, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia, and subsequently died of SFTS. Her 31-year-old granddaughter, who had an open wound on her hand, cared for the patient and cleaned her urine. Eleven days later, she developed fever, nausea, vomiting, headache, fatigue, and myalgia. Laboratory tests confirmed SFTS virus infection by RT-PCR, with an initial cycle threshold (Ct) value of 38.85, which subsequently decreased to 31.48 over the following 2 days, indicating active viral replication. She recovered after antiviral therapy and was discharged on July 7. Comprehensive epidemiological investigation ruled out other potential transmission routes, including blood contact, tick bites, and environmental exposure. However, direct virological evidence from the index patient's urine and genomic sequencing to confirm viral homology between the two cases were not available. CONCLUSION: This report describes a probable human-to-human SFTS transmission event associated with urine exposure through an open wound. While the absence of direct virological and genomic evidence precludes definitive confirmation, the convergence of epidemiological, clinical, and temporal evidence strongly supports this transmission route. This case highlights the need for enhanced protective measures-particularly the use of gloves when handling any body fluids, including urine-during care of SFTS patients.

content.title: Variable transmission efficiency of mammalian origin HPAI D1.1 H5N1 strains in ferrets.
content.abstract: AbstractHighly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 2.3.4.4b genotype D1.1 lineage continues to predominate in the United States wild bird population and has spilled over into dairy cattle three independent times. To assess the transmission risk of this sublineage, we performed direct-contact transmission experiments for three distinct D1.1 strains in ferrets. Two of these strains were isolated from humans and one from a lethal cat infection. We found that only one human isolate (A/NV/10/2025) was able to transmit efficiently between ferrets. Compared to the other strains, this isolate harbored the mammalian adaptive PB2 D701N mutation, suggesting this mutation may be a candidate contributing to enhanced transmission efficiency of D1.1 as opposed to the PB2 E627 K substitution present in the lethal cat isolate. Based on these data we conclude that the transmission fitness of D1.1 strains is modest but special attention should be paid to emergence of adaptation at the PB2 701 position.

content.title: Pfcrt copy number amplification detected in a Plasmodium falciparum outbreak.
content.abstract: Antimalarial resistance is one of the greatest threats to malaria elimination. Following an outbreak of Plasmodium falciparum infection in Sabah Malaysia in 2019, 98 samples were sequenced to search for adaptations driving the outbreak. The genomic data revealed evidence of clonal expansion of a strain carrying multiple copies of the chloroquine resistance transporter gene ( pfcrt ) in 86 cases. A TaqMan qPCR assay was developed to quantify pfcrt copy number, confirming the in silico evidence of duplication. Whilst point mutations in pfcrt have been associated with resistance to chloroquine and other drugs, copy number amplification has not been widely explored as a resistance mechanism. We investigated the genetic architecture of the duplication, revealing a wildtype haplotype (3D7 reference-type with 76K variant) and a novel mutant (with 76T mutation). Application of the TaqMan assay in 65 P. falciparum cases from neighbouring Palawan Island, the Philippines, identified a further two cases with pfcrt duplication. Assessment of the global genomic data in the MalariaGEN Pf8 repository identified a further 86 cases, including 73 (85%) from West Africa with evidence of pfcrt duplication. Amongst 47 monoclonal MalariaGEN cases, majority (95%) comprised wild type and mutant variants at codon 76. Our study reveals a potential previously unconsidered antimalarial resistance mechanism for P. falciparum and provides an assay for surveillance in other populations.

content.title: Rising spillover risk: Lessons from the Andes hantavirus outbreak.
content.abstract: The unprecedented expansion of human activity boundaries is turning spillover from a chance event into a foreseeable ecological and epidemiological certainty. Using the 2026 Andes hantavirus cruise ship outbreak as an entry point, this study examines it within a broader driver framework: nearly all emerging infectious disease events in humans in recent decades have originated from wildlife transmission; under climate-change and land-use scenarios, approximately 3139 mammal species are projected to aggregate in new combinations by 2070, causing an estimated 4000 cross-species viral transmission events. The rapid expansion of tourism into ecologically fragile regions - sub-Antarctic waters, the deep sea, and primary forests - the persistence of habitat fragmentation and animal trade, and the reshaping of wildlife distribution and vector dynamics by extreme climate events together constitute "novel contact amplifiers" that accelerate contact at the human-animal-environment interface. Robotics, artificial intelligence, autonomous driving, and automated logistics are extending human activities into previously inaccessible regions, yet they remain almost entirely absent from current spillover risk assessments. The limitations of cruise ship medical systems - whose core capacity lies in "recognize, isolate, stabilize, and transfer" rather than definitive diagnosis and treatment - were fully exposed in this event. From a One Health perspective, this paper proposes that responses to spillover risk must shift from passive reaction to proactive interface governance, incorporate technology-driven increases in contact frequency into prevention and control frameworks, and advance cornerstone strategies such as broad-spectrum vaccines and broad-spectrum antiviral drugs at the basic research level.

content.title: COVID 19 and fungal infection - A double disaster:a case series.
content.abstract: The recent Coronavirus pandemic in 2019 [COVID-19] was associated with an increased risk of opportunistic fungal co-infection. This case series presents 5 autopsy-confirmed fungal co-infections identified in patients who died following COVID-19. Among the notable findings were Fusarium-associated fungal myocarditis and human infection with Hormographiella, an extremely rare pathogen found in COVID-19. To the best of our knowledge, the latter represents the first reported fungal co-infection with this pathogen in COVID-19. We also report the first postmortem diagnosis of invasive pulmonary mucormycosis in COVID-19 in Sri Lanka, confirmed with culture as Rhizopus spp. Postmortem examination, histopathological analysis and fungal culture revealed fungal infections that had not been suspected clinically or had been only partially characterized, and provided the microbiological and pathological evidence necessary for establishing the cause of death These findings highlight the medicolegal importance of thorough autopsy examination in severe COVID-19, especially in situations where opportunistic fungal infection may have contributed to death.

content.title: The role of psychological inflexibility on post-traumatic stress symptoms among COVID-19 survivors.
content.abstract: BACKGROUND: The COVID-19 outbreak spread rapidly around the world, causing a pandemic and negatively affecting the mental health of society. During this process, one of the most mentally affected groups has been patients who contracted COVID-19. Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is reported to be an important public health problem after pandemics. In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between psychological inflexibility, which is thought to underlie mental problems and PTSD symptoms in Covid-19 survivors. METHODS: A total of 194 patients over 18 years old who were admitted to the Chest Diseases Outpatient Clinic with a previous COVID-19 infection and who agreed to participate were included in the study. Socio-demographic information form as well as questionnaire forms for Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), Acceptance and Action Questionnaire II (AAQ-II), Impact of Events Scale-Revised (IES-R) and Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) were conducted on the patients. RESULTS: Female gender, participants with lower education level, and those with additional chronic diseases had significantly higher IES-R values (p = 0.014, p = 0.029 and p = 0.011, respectively). IES-R scores showed a significant positive correlation with HADS-Anxiety (A) (p < 0.001), HADS-Depression (D) (p < 0.001), AAQ-II (p < 0.001) and ISI (p < 0.001) scores. AAQ-II also scores significantly associated with HADS-A scores (p = 0.0053), and similarly, the effect of HADS-A scores on IES-R scores was also significant (p = 0.0009). The mediating role of HADS-A scores in the effect of AAQ-II scores on IES-R scores was significant (β = 0.0757, 95% CI = 0.0024 to 0.1785). AAQ-II scores had a significantly associated with ISI scores (β = 0.1263, p = 0.0033). Similarly, ISI scores had a significant association with IES-R scores (β = 1.3882, p < 0.001). In this model, ISI scores significantly mediated the relationship between AAQ-II scores and IES-R scores (β = 0.1753, 95% CI = 0.0640 to 0.3060). CONCLUSION: In our study, we found that female gender, low education level and additional chronic diseases were associated with PTSD symptoms in COVID-19 survivors. We also found that psychological inflexibility may be a common factor associated with PTSD, depression and anxiety symptoms and insomnia severity. Psychotherapeutic interventions to reduce psychological inflexibility, especially in patients who suffered an infection like COVID-19 during the pandemics, may prevent these patients from experiencing anxiety, depression, PTSD symptoms and sleep problems.

content.title: Antifungal Resistance and Adhesin-Mediated Phenotypic Plasticity Among Genomically Diverse Candida auris Clinical Isolates.
content.abstract: Candida auris (currently Candidozyma auris ) is an emerging fungal pathogen responsible for dramatic global increase in invasive candidiasis with high mortality. Most concerning, C. auris has a high propensity to colonize patients and persist and develop multidrug resistance to main classes of antifungals. In this study, we investigated the genetic and phenotypic diversity and resistance mechanisms of C. auris clinical isolates recovered from hospitalized infected patients. A total of 53 isolates from 38 unique patients were recovered from various clinical sources and evaluated for susceptibility to routine antifungal drugs. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis were performed to generate a phylogenetic network to infer population structure and identify mutations associated with drug resistance development. Isolates were also phenotypically evaluated for ability to form biofilms and aggregate, and cell wall adhesins gene expression studies were performed to provide mechanistic insights into C. auris phenotypic plasticity. Except for one clade III isolate, all isolates belonged to clade I and all were resistant to fluconazole with incidence of resistance to amphotericin B, echinocandins or both. Non-synonymous SNPs were found in genes associated with antifungal resistance including ERG11, TAC1B, CDR1 and FKS1 . Phenotypically, isolates varied in their ability to form biofilm and aggregate which correlated with expression of the Scf1 and Als4112 cell wall adhesins genes highlighting C. auris phenotypic plasticity in circulating clinical strains. These findings underscore the growing clinical threat posed by C. auris and reinforce the need for optimized surveillance and treatment strategies for controlling its spread.

content.title: Bovine mammary tissues are susceptible to infection by viruses bearing panzootic H5N1 influenza A virus glycoproteins.
content.abstract: The emergence of the panzootic clade 2.3.4.4b highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza in 2020 marked a major expansion in the host range of influenza A viruses (IAVs), raising concerns about further cross-species transmission events and zoonotic spillover. The introduction of 2.3.4.4b viruses into US dairy herds has resulted in widespread circulation, accompanied by reduced milk yield, mastitis and high viral loads in milk. Notably, virus circulation in dairy cattle represents a novel route for mammalian adaptation and transmission that has already led to more than 40 human cases in the USA since 2024. As haemagglutinin (HA) is the primary determinant of viral host range and tissue tropism, we investigated whether viruses containing the glycoproteins of avian H5N1 subclade 2.3.4.4b viruses could infect mammary tissue from Aberdeen Angus, Holstein Friesian and Limousin cattle. Using mammary gland explants, we inoculated tissues with attenuated reassortant viruses expressing the HA and neuraminidase (NA) of three 2.3.4.4b viruses that predated the emergence of H5N1 in the US cattle: A/chicken/England/053052/2021 (AIV07), A/chicken/Scotland/054477/2021 (AIV09) and A/chicken/England/085598/2022 (AIV48). Detection of viral NP antigen by immunohistochemistry in explants from both the teat and gland cistern for all three breeds following inoculation with AIV09 and AIV48 indicates that mammary tissue from each of the three tested cattle breeds is susceptible to infection by viruses bearing H5N1 glycoproteins. Lectin staining showed expression of both α2,3- and α2,6-linked sialic acids in the mammary tissue of all donors, indicating that all three breeds have the potential to support infection with both avian- and mammalian-adapted IAVs. Together, these findings demonstrate that the mammary glands from both beef and dairy cattle breeds are susceptible to infection with viruses bearing avian-origin H5N1 glycoproteins and suggest that bovine mammary tissue may provide an environment in which diverse IAVs could co-infect the same tissue. This possibility underscores the need for further investigation and the inclusion of both beef and dairy cattle in ongoing H5N1 surveillance and risk-assessment frameworks.

content.title: Lessons Learned During the 2024‒2025 Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Virus Outbreak Response in the United States: The Experience of State and Local Public Health Departments.
content.abstract: Objectives. To describe challenges and lessons learned during state and local health department responses to the 2024‒2025 highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) outbreaks. Methods. We conducted semistructured interviews from August to November 2025 with Department of Health and Agriculture staff from states with confirmed or probable A(H5N1) human cases. We conducted 15 total interviews with 37 participants from 10 US states. Interview transcripts were inductively and deductively coded to identify generalizable lessons that might improve future outbreak response efforts. Results. Key themes included difficulty accessing farms and reaching at-risk populations; lack of sufficient guidelines for proactively responding to zoonotic outbreaks that could have human health implications; the importance of maintaining preparedness planning, capacity, and infrastructure; and uncertainty around future capacity to respond to outbreaks because of resource constraints and changes in federal leadership. Conclusions. Although this study focused on responses to A(H5N1) outbreaks, the findings are indicative of the nation's overall readiness for biological threats. Prioritization of capacity building for infectious disease outbreaks, including robust health department funding to support continued disease surveillance, is critical to prevent more widespread transmission. (Am J Public Health. Published online ahead of print September 3, 2026:e1-e7. https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2026.308656).

content.title: Epidemiology of Chikungunya Virus Infection in the Philippines.
content.abstract: Background: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) has circulated in the Philippines for more than six decades. We systematically reviewed the epidemiology of CHIKV in the Philippines, integrating evidence on transmission, seroprevalence, diagnostics and molecular lineages. Methods: We searched PubMed and Embase to March 2026 for original studies reporting incidence, prevalence, seroprevalence, outbreak characteristics, or surveillance findings in human populations in the Philippines. The gray literature from the Department of Health (DOH) Epidemiology Bureau's national chikungunya surveillance (2018-March 2026) was included separately. Findings were synthesized narratively because of substantial heterogeneity. Results: Sixteen studies and one national surveillance dataset were included. National surveillance recorded 12,662 cases from 2018 to early 2026, including 722 laboratory-confirmed cases and three fatalities. The Asian genotype predominated during the 2011-2013 epidemic, while Indian Ocean lineage (IOL) viruses were detected in southern Mindanao. Conclusions: Transmission of CHIKV in the Philippines is mostly sporadic with periods of low-level transmission. Because the clinical features overlap with dengue, acute febrile illness surveillance should test for both viruses.

content.title: One Health preparedness for Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus: lessons from the 2026 outbreak centred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
content.abstract: The 2026 outbreak of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), caused by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), involved limited international exportation but remained centred in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The outbreak tested whether earlier institutional mobilisation translated into timely field delivery. We conducted a structured narrative review of peer-reviewed research, official reports and operational guidance on epidemiology, diagnostics, medical countermeasures (MCMs), One Health surveillance, clinical care, infection prevention and control (IPC), community engagement and cross-border preparedness. Key institutional mechanisms for emergency decision-making, coordination and MCM prioritisation were activated earlier than during the 2013-2016 Ebola virus disease epidemic in West Africa, widening the window for action. Field delivery nevertheless remained uneven: the model-adjusted median onset-to-sampling delay was 4.8 days among 129 confirmed patients, while insecurity posed additional challenges for field response. Preparedness was further constrained by uncertainty about reservoir ecology, limited clinical validation of BDBV-specific diagnostics and the absence of MCMs with established efficacy in BVD. We therefore propose a One Health alert-to-action pathway linking human, animal, environmental and community signals to BDBV-inclusive confirmation, safe care, IPC, cross-border continuity, accountable governance and feedback-informed adaptation. Earlier activation is a preparedness gain, but protection depends on whether that advantage is carried through reliable, traceable and equitable operational hand-offs.

content.title: Identification of key COVID-19 infection contexts over time and the importance of within household infections.
content.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Infectious disease outbreaks, most recently the COVID-19 pandemic, have broad societal impacts and may require the introduction of costly non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). To minimize these burdens, the identification of infection contexts is paramount: knowing where infections occur allows the determination of high-risk environments, the identification of outbreak sources, and finally the introduction of targeted, and thus cost-efficient NPIs. METHODS: Starting in February 2020, the Cologne public health department interviewed all PCR-confirmed COVID-19 cases residing in Cologne regarding their probable infection context. The collected individual-level data was entered into an in-house-developed software. From these interviews, aggregated case numbers for the different infection contexts are available at the daily level. The manuscript provides an explorative analysis of the aggregated data. RESULTS: During 2021, within-one's-own-household was the dominant known infection context in Cologne. Following within-own-household-infections, the contributions differed over time, with notable contributions of shared accommodations (specifically nursing homes) early in the year, large contributions of disease import during the summer of 2021, and increasing contributions of family (different household) and leisure miscellaneous over the course of 2021. CONCLUSION: The analysis reveals that the combination of state-mandated NPIs and voluntary behavior adaptations strongly influenced the regional spreading dynamics and managed to limit infections in critical contexts, such as nursing homes.

content.title: New WHO technical package to help countries improve health data for COVID-19 response and beyond
content.abstract: Today, as part of its commitment to strengthening health information systems and improving health[1], especially in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, WHO announced a new approach to improving access to life-saving data: the SCORE for Health Data Technical Package. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the urgent need for timely and reliable data to drive strategic health action. Too many countries still lack both the infrastructure to routinely gather health data and the analytical capacity to use these data for effective health actions and emergency response. “Countries must be able to measure progress to make progress,” said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. “Particularly during COVID-19, reliable data is the best way to coordinate response efforts and improve health in all areas.” Accurate health data are necessary to understand specific country needs in order to improve health and save lives. Data also helps direct scarce resources to where they are needed most. The SCORE (Survey, Count, Optimize, Review, Enable) Technical Package aims to improve the availability of timely, reliable, validated, and comparable health data. For the first time in a single, harmonized package, it represents all the key elements for optimized health information system performance. Simply put, SCORE will help governments around the globe set benchmarks and improve standards in healthcare. In response to the challenges of data availability highlighted in the WHO World Health Statistics 2020 report, SCORE includes more than 90 universally-accepted tools and standards for health information systems strengthening. “Using data to inform public health priorities and strategies has never been more important,” said Dr Kelly Henning, Director of Public Health Programs at Bloomberg Philanthropies[2]. “The SCORE Technical Package provides country governments around the world with high-quality, essential technical guidance so that countries can strengthen their own data systems.” WHO is proud to partner with the Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health Initiative to deliver this timely resource to countries. Below are some examples of how SCORE can improve individual lives and communities: The birth of a child is registered so they can access essential health services, attend school, and apply for a passport; A death is registered with cause-of-death accurately captured so that policy-makers have a better understanding of all-cause and COVID-specific mortality and associated risk factors and implement programs and policies to save lives; Health data are disaggregated by age, sex and cause of death to illustrate the root causes of health disparities and help direct resources to the most vulnerable groups such as those who do not speak the local language or face stigma and discrimination in their community; Health facilities have the capacity to regularly measure the quality of their services, workforce and patient data and can make a compelling case for increased funding to national and international stakeholders; Health data are integrated with other sectors so that social determinants of health such as pollution, sanitation and nutrition are addressed to reduce the overall burden of disease. The package's initial release includes two documents: SCORE Essential Interventions – including an overview of health information systems, underlying elements, and indicators to assess progress with sample actions; and SCORE Tools and Standards -- including resources to address critical health data gaps and strengthen country health data. “We must keep score to save lives. WHO is committed to working with countries and partners to rapidly scale up capacity for data collection and use in order to improve policy and performance,” added Dr Samira Asma, Assistant Director-General for Data, Analytics and Delivery for Impact at WHO. “We must act now to invest in statistical systems in countries, respond to this pandemic and meet the SDGs and the Triple Billion targets. Our window of opportunity is closing, and we cannot wait to address data gaps. Data use to address country needs has to be a priority today.” Country-owned, disaggregated data will be essential for more resilient and sustainable health systems going forward. COVID-19 is both a wake-up call and a stark reminder of the challenges we still have to address. But it is also an opportunity to build back better through solidarity, information-sharing and collaboration. SCORE is one example of how a collaborative approach can benefit countries by providing a common set of tools based on shared standards. This package is designed to be practical, actionable and flexible. We will only be successful in combatting COVID-19 if we work together. Future components of the SCORE Technical Package are due to be released later this year, including the SCORE Assessment Instrument and global, regional and country status reports. Together, these will provide a complete package of information to plan and monitor progress against national and subnational priorities as well as global targets. ----- [1] https://www.who.int/about/what-we-do/thirteenth-general-programme-of-work-2019---2023#:~:text=The%20Thirteenth%20General%20Programme%20of,health%20at%20the%20country%20leve [2] Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health Initiative provided funding to support the SCORE for Health Data Technical Package

content.title: Trimester-dependent vertical transmission of H5N1 influenza virus through placental and mammary routes impairs offspring development.
content.abstract: Avian influenza H5N1 has pandemic potential and historically causes more severe disease in pregnant women than the general population. With increasing transmission of H5N1 detected among placental mammals, animal models are necessary for testing countermeasures, including during pregnancy. Pregnant outbred mice infected with a contemporary strain of bovine H5N1 during the second trimester equivalent causes in utero transmission, with infectious virus detected in the uterus, placenta, and fetus. Birth following third trimester infection results in offspring with decreased size, neurodevelopmental delays, and adolescent behavioral impairments, with infectious virus detected in the neonatal milk ring and lungs, as well as mammary tissues. H5N1 viral protein colocalizes with trophoblast cells in the placenta and epithelial cells in mammary tissue that spatially overlap with lectins for α2,3-linked SA. With the pandemic potential of H5N1, our vertical transmission model in placental mammals is essential for understanding viral spread and evaluating treatments during pregnancy.

content.title: H5N1 epidemiology and production impact in eight California dairy herds at the outbreak epicenter.
content.abstract: The 2024 emergence of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) H5N1, clade 2.3.4.4b, genotype B3.13, in U.S. dairy cattle was a novel disease event affecting animal health, production, and public health. We conducted structured interviews with managers of eight H5N1-positive dairies in Tulare County, California, the epicenter of the 2024 outbreak, covering a 30-day reference period, the first quarantine, the 30 days following quarantine release, and, for two dairies, a second quarantine. Given the small sample, we used descriptive statistics with Multiple Factor Analysis and hierarchical clustering to explore herd heterogeneity. Mean milk yield declined modestly (2.6%) during early quarantine but recovered above baseline by release; somatic cell count rose 21% and remained elevated. Three-quarters of dairies reported abnormal milk appearance, all experienced reduced feed intake (~8%) and pregnancy losses, and mortality in lactating cows averaged 1.5%. Biosecurity improvements were largely reactive rather than preventive. Exploratory multivariate analyses identified two underlying dimensions and three distinct herd profiles differing in production, clinical course, and biosecurity intensity. In this work, H5N1 infection was associated with variable but measurable impacts on production, mammary health, and reproduction; findings are consistent with reports from other states but warrant confirmation in larger, more diverse studies.

content.title: Minimised SARS-CoV-2 transmission during Tokyo 2020 Olympic and Paralympic Games: insights from enhanced integrated surveillance, Japan, July to September 2021.
content.abstract: BACKGROUNDAmid the COVID-19 pandemic, stringent public health measures were taken during the Tokyo 2020 Olympic and Paralympic Games (Tokyo 2020).AIMWe describe SARS-CoV-2 transmission among Games participants and in-person contributors (GPIPC)s.METHODSTokyo 2020-related SARS-CoV-2 infection cases were individuals linked to the event, testing positive for the virus between 1 July-19 September 2021, reported to the Tokyo Metropolitan Government. Attack rates among athletes and team officials were determined. Enhanced case-based surveillance integrating genomic sequencing data supported viral spread investigations among various GPIPC groups.RESULTSA total 804 cases (median age: 35 years, interquartile range (IQR): 27-45; 194 female/610 male) were reported. Among athletes and team officials, attack rates were 0.6% (65/11,400) in Olympic Games and 0.6% (30/4,800) in Paralympic Games. These 95 infections concerned mainly overseas travellers (n = 92), 85 of whom were diagnosed within 14 days of arrival in Japan. Among the 804 cases, whole-genome sequencing data were obtained for 304 (median age: 38 years, IQR: 29-47; 67 female/237 male) with sufficient viral load (as indicated by RT-PCR Cq ≤ 32), including 79% (75/95) of athletes and team officials cases, 74% (131/176) of Games' organisers and media cases, and ˂ 20% (98/533) of remaining cases. Delta variants dominated (94%; 285/304), with domestic (AY.29 lineage) Delta strains prominent among Delta-variant-affected resident cases (96%; 104/108) and Games' organisers and media cases diagnosed ≥ 15 days after entering Japan (97%; 63/65). Overseas Delta strains mostly affected travellers within 14 days of entry, particularly athletes and team officials (97%; 66/68) and Games' organisers and media (29/34).CONCLUSIONMultilayered-risk-reduction measures likely minimised SARS-CoV-2 transmission to athletes.

content.title: Epidemiological update on spatial and space-time clusters of African swine fever in the Philippines.
content.abstract: African swine fever (ASF), particularly the highly contagious Genotype II strain, is a transboundary viral disease causing up to 100% mortality in swine and threatening food security across the Asia-Pacific region. Since 2019, control strategies in the Philippines have relied on depopulation and strict administrative zoning to limit contiguous, land-based spread. However, the long-term effectiveness of these approaches within the country's fragmented archipelagic landscape remains poorly understood, complicating evidence-based resource allocation and preparedness for regional vaccination campaigns. Here we show that the endemic trajectory of ASF was highly non-uniform across the three main island groups of the Philippines from October 2022 to October 2024. Spatiotemporal analysis of a national surveillance dataset comprising 8,213 barangay-level events revealed twelve statistically significant retrospective space-time clusters-with radii up to 183.2 kilometers-and highly asynchronous regional epidemic waves across Luzon, the Visayas, and Mindanao. Although crude case volumes were highest in Luzon (52.10%), followed by the Visayas (31.69%) and Mindanao (16.21%), accounting for swine population density reshaped the spatial distribution. Spatial mapping and a Getis-Ord Gi* hotspot analysis consistently identified the highest burden of reported ASF events within Regions IV-A, IV-B, and VI, specifically peaking on Mindoro Island and in the Western Visayas. Together, these findings demonstrate that maritime borders fail to provide natural biosecurity isolation against transboundary viral transmission. Consequently, region-specific interventions and resources must be dynamically allocated to address this heterogeneous spatial burden. These spatiotemporal results provide the evidence-based framework necessary to transition toward targeted sub-national surveillance and to systematically evaluate the epidemiological impact and guide live-attenuated vaccine implementation in the Philippines and analogous archipelagic settings throughout the Asia-Pacific.

content.title: Multiple introductions and spread of novel reassortant highly pathogenic avian influenza A (H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses via wild birds, South Korea, 2024-2025.
content.abstract: Between 14 October 2024 and 24 March 2025, 43 cases of clade 2.3.4.4b highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) type A (H5N1) infections in wild birds and 1 case in a leopard cat were detected through the national HPAI surveillance program. We performed whole-genome sequencing of 51 isolates and investigated their phylogenetic relationships. Phylogenetic analyses identified nine distinct genotypes, designated Kor24-25A to Kor24-25I. The most commonly detected genotype, Kor24-25A (n = 24), was frequently detected in Pelecaniformes and was most prevalent between December 2024 and January 2025. Bayesian continuous and discrete trait phylodynamic analyses using HA gene sequences identified the three most probable routes of viral introduction via Gyeonggi, Jeju, and the southern coastal areas of the Korean Peninsula and suggested that wild ducks served as the primary reservoirs facilitating viral transmission in the wild bird population. During the 2024-2025 season, great egrets (Ardea alba) appeared to be more frequently affected than other wild bird species, suggesting possible seasonal differences in species-specific disease outcomes among wild birds. This study provides valuable insights into the phylodynamics, host associations, and transmission patterns of HPAI H5N1 viruses. It emphasizes the importance of enhanced surveillance programs targeting key avian hosts and high-risk geographic areas.

WOAH calls on its Members to strengthen surveillance, early warning and preparedness for vector-borne diseases (VBDs). A vector-borne disease is a disease that can be transmitted from one animal or person to another through a living organism, known as a vector. Vectors are most often insects, such as mosquitoes, ticks, fleas or sandflies, which can carry and transmit pathogens. Analysis of official reports submitted through the World Animal Health Information System (WAHIS) shows a steady increase of the frequency (incidence) of some of these VDBs and the overall number of countries reporting these diseases. Vector-borne diseases are currently showing a marked change in global distribution, with climate change acting as an important driver, alongside anthropogenic factors, vectors ecology, ecological disruption, higher mobility of animals and humans. Analysis of official information reported through WAHIS indicates a marked increase in reported exceptional epidemiological events for several VBDs with important implications for animal health, biodiversity conservation, food security, livelihoods and the resilience of Veterinary Services worldwide. A marked rise since 2023 Data reported through WAHIS reveal a marked rise in VBDs notified to WOAH through WAHIS from 2023 onward, concentrated in a small number of diseases and countries. Bluetongue accounts for the largest amount of this increase, with an average of 38 exceptional epidemiological events per year recorded in 2023–2025 compared with an average of 9.1 events per year between 2015 and 2022 — driven mainly by the incursion of the BTV-3 serotype into north-western Europe beginning in autumn 2023. West Nile fever (a zoonosis that can cause encephalitis in humans) events increased substantially from 8.0 per year on average to 55 per year. Equine infectious anemia showed more moderate increase, led by an increase in reporting of cases in countries in the Americas. By contrast, other listed vector-borne diseases, including lumpy skin disease , have generally remained close to their historical baseline in term of number of exceptional epidemiological events, but have significantly increased their geographic range from Africa to Middle East, Europe and Asia. Since 2005, bluetongue alone has accounted for the majority of all VBD outbreaks reported to WOAH, with lumpy skin disease the next most frequently reported. Regional patterns vary considerably. Since 2022, Europe has reported the overwhelming majority of bluetongue outbreaks, while Africa has remained the primary region affected by Rift Valley fever, and the Americas have accounted for the majority of equine infectious anemia and western equine encephalitis cases. These data should be interpreted as trends in reported events , rather than as a direct measure of changes in disease incidence. Changes in surveillance intensity, diagnostic capacity and notification practices can influence reporting alongside genuine changes in disease occurrence and distribution. Climate change as a structural driver The observed trends are consistent with the demonstrated relationship between climate change and vector ecology highlighted in WOAH’s 2025 State of the World’s Animal Health report . Rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns and land-use modifications are altering vector density, activity periods, survival and geographical range. In some areas, conditions may allow vectors to reproduce throughout the year, substantially extending their activity period and increasing opportunities for pathogen transmission. These changes can create conditions favourable to the establishment or transmission of VBDs into previously unaffected, often temperate, regions. WOAH reporting has documented changes in the geographical distribution of several VBDs, including an increase in the maximum latitude at which outbreaks have been reported. Other factors—including ecological change, unregulated animal movements and trade, and changes in wildlife–livestock–human interactions—can also influence VBD emergence and spread. Many of the vectors involved pathogens that affect both animals and humans, reinforcing the need for surveillance and response that spans the animal–human–environment interface. Some vector-borne diseases involve complex interactions between animals, humans, vectors and the environment. Effective prevention and control require an integrated One Health approach involving Veterinary Services, public health authorities, environmental agencies, research institutions and other relevant stakeholders. Control options may be limited, with vaccination being an effective measure where available. Other preventive measures include reducing vector breeding sites, using mechanical protection and, where appropriate, repellents. Environmental insecticide use should be carefully considered due to potential impacts on non-target organisms and ecosystems. Continued research is also needed to develop and evaluate biological control approaches. WOAH’s international standards — including the Terrestrial Code recommendations on surveillance for arthropod vectors — provide the scientific foundation for Members to assess vector presence, distribution and abundance, and to design surveillance strategies proportionate to risk. WOAH also supports its Members through innovative early-warning approaches. Since 2022, the PROVNA project has worked with Veterinary Services in North Africa to combine earth observation and climate data with disease occurrence data reported through WAHIS. The project is building models capable of identifying areas with environmental and climatic characteristics suitable for VBDs presence and transmission. Such approaches demonstrate how transdisciplinary collaboration between epidemiologists, entomologists, data scientists and Veterinary Services can shift disease response from reactive to anticipatory. WOAH calls on its Members to: Strengthen integrated surveillance and early warning , combining vector, disease and environmental data to detect changes in distribution, abundance and transmission risk at an early stage before they escalate; Report vector-borne disease events promptly and transparently through the World Animal Health Information System (WAHIS), including relevant information on serotypes and strains where available; Invest in entomological, laboratory and diagnostic capacity , including within national Veterinary Services and in collaboration with WOAH Reference Centres, to sustain vector monitoring and disease surveillance over the long term; Adopt risk-based, science-based control measures , including timely vaccination with quality-assured and epidemiologically appropriate vaccines, vector control and movement management, adapted to the local ecology and epidemiological situation; Strengthen cross-sectoral and cross-border collaboration , including through regional networks and initiatives such as PROVNA, GF-TADs, VectorNet, MediLabSecure among others and the Quadripartite One Health activities, to anticipate and respond to vectors that do not recognise national boundaries; and Facilitate safe trade through science-based measures , ensuring that import risk management measures are proportionate to the identified risk and consistent with WOAH International Standards. As several factors mentioned above continue to reshape the ecology of disease vectors, investment in surveillance, laboratory capacity and Veterinary Services is essential not only for animal health but also for food security, livelihood, biodiversity protection, as well as global health security. WOAH remains committed to supporting its Members through its international standards, expert networks, data systems and scientific collaboration to anticipate, prevent and respond to vector-borne disease evolving threat. content.title: First autochthonous cases of Oropouche fever in Southern Brazil: A case series in a non-endemic area, Santa Catarina, 2024.
content.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To describe time, person, and place of the first Oropouche fever confirmed in the state of Santa Catarina, evaluating their autochthonism. METHODS: A descriptive case series study conducted with residents of five Santa Catarina municipalities, who tested positive for Oropouche fever in laboratory tests between April 25 and June 12, 2024. Retrospective samples, negative for dengue, and viable for molecular analysis (RT-PCR) were considered. Secondary data collected during epidemiological investigations and information systems were used. Statistical analysis was performed on SPSS 18.0. Autochthonous cases were defined as those with no travel history 15 days prior to symptoms onset. RESULTS: Of the 41 eligible cases, 33 participated in the study. Most were female (63.6%), white (63.6%) and of economically active age (78.8%). Most frequent symptoms included headache (93.9%), fever (90.9%) and myalgia (81.8%). About half reported recurrence of symptoms after clinical cure. Most reported exposure to waterbodies (57.6%) and areas with natural vegetation (48.5%), as well as frequent presence of the Culicoides sp. in homes and workplaces. Most lived and worked near environments conducive to vector proliferation such as agricultural areas with banana cultivation. No case reported travel to other federative units or abroad. CONCLUSION: Oropouche cases in Santa Catarina presented a clinical-epidemiological profile compatible with previous descriptions. Unprecedented detection of the Oropouche virus in the region reinforces the need for timely diagnosis and integrated surveillance for emerging and reemerging arboviruses in Brazil.

content.title: Urotensin II: A Key Role in Hormonal and Inflammatory Cytokine Regulation in COVID-19 Patients.
content.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic exhibits a wide spectrum of severities and pathophysiological mechanisms. The virus targets angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors, disrupting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) balance, which may explain various symptoms and risk factors. Fibrosis of the small airways is pivotal in the emergence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Understanding these complex pathophysiological mechanisms is crucial for developing effective treatments and personalized approaches for COVID-19 patients. The present study is aimed at analyzing the concentrations of the clinical and laboratory parameters-such as hematological, biochemical, serological, angiotensin II (ANG II), endothelin-1 (ET-1), urotensin II (UII), and cortisol parameters-in patients with SARS-CoV-2 and evaluating the elevation of these parameters related to the pathogenicity. The study included two distinct groups: a healthy control group (n = 25) and a COVID-19 patient group (n = 75) during the period from August 2021 to January 2022. Cytokine levels were evaluated using commercially available enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. The comparative analysis revealed that severe cases of COVID-19 have a significant elevation in the concentrations of hematological, biochemical, serological, and hormonal levels such as ANG II, ET-1, UII, and cortisol, as well as a substantial decline in the concentration of LYM%, in comparison with mild cases of COVID-19 and the control groups. Based on these findings, we concluded that ET-1, ANG II, and UII may be associated with COVID-19 pathophysiology and are linked to endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and thrombosis.
